articles.title: Case File No. 005 — Stanford Steve: GameDay's best picker
articles.dek: Twelve years of tracked picks. 648–529 against the spread. Plus 60 units. The numbers say the guy next to the headgear is the sharpest voice on the set — with one glaring exception.
articles.author: Fade Cases

fadeCard.caption: Stanford Steve · Tail him (on Saturdays)
fadeCard.slipTitle: The tracked record · via Cole's Gameday Blog

picks.t: Highest win rate of any 1,000-pick analyst tracked

body: Every Saturday morning, Steve Coughlin — Stanford Steve to anyone with a TV — sits at the College GameDay desk and gives out numbers. Unlike most people who do that for a living, his have been written down. All of them. For twelve years.

Cole's Gameday Blog has tracked every public pick Coughlin has made since 2014 — GameDay, ESPN's betting shows, SportsCenter, all of it. The ledger: 648 wins, 529 losses, 24 pushes against the spread. That's 55.1% over 1,201 picks — and at standard juice it works out to more than 60 units of profit. For context, the break-even line for a bettor paying -110 is 52.4%. Holding three points above that for over a decade is not luck. It's a career.

The comparison table is where it gets impressive. Among every analyst the site has tracked to 1,000-plus picks, nobody matches his win rate — not the touts, not the sharps-on-TV, nobody. Only one picker on the entire board has banked more total units, and it took him three times the volume to do it.

The peaks are real too: a 57–29 season in 2018 worth almost 23 units, a 53–30 debut year in 2014, and this season he's already 63–50 and up 7.4 units through the first stretch — including eating a loss on Clemson +10 against LSU in Week 1 like everyone else who trusted the Tigers' opponent.

Now the asterisk, because the receipts cut both ways: on NFL Sundays, Stanford Steve is mortal. His tracked pro record is 166–162–7 — under 51%, eleven units in the red. The same man who prints money on college football gives it back on the NFL. If ever a bettor was built for a Tail button on Saturdays and a Fade button on Sundays, it's him.

That's the whole thesis of Fade in one human being: records are real, context is everything, and knowing who is actually good — on which sport, in which spot — is the edge. When GameDay's board drops on Saturday, you'll know exactly what his number is worth.
Source: Cole's Gameday Blog (gamedaycole.com) — tracked pick data for Steve Coughlin, 2014–2026. Records reflect publicly posted picks at standard -110 pricing unless noted.

articles.title: LSU is betting on themselves — literally
articles.dek: Five Kalshi block trades, $662,050 down, up to $3 million back — rung for rung, the exact shape of Lane Kiffin's playoff bonus ladder. Welcome to the era where the school's insurer is holding tickets on the season.
articles.author: Fade Desk

fadeCard.slipTitle: The hedge · five Kalshi block trades

picks.t: LSU makes the College Football Playoff — pays $837,500
LSU reaches the national title game
LSU wins the national championship — total pays $3M

body: Lane Kiffin's LSU contract pays him bonuses that climb with every step of a playoff run — $750,000 just for getting the Tigers in, scaling to $3 million if he wins the whole thing. Someone is on the hook for that money. And that someone just went to the window.

Two weeks before the reports surfaced, five block trades — large positions negotiated off-exchange — hit the prediction market Kalshi, all on LSU's season: make the College Football Playoff, reach the quarterfinal, reach the semifinal, reach the title game, win the national championship. Cost of the position: $662,050. Maximum payout if the Tigers run the table: $3 million. That is not a round number by accident — it is, to the dollar, Kiffin's championship bonus.

The trades trace to Game Point Capital, a sports insurance firm whose entire business is insuring schools against the happy disaster of their coach hitting his bonuses. Kalshi's CEO announced a partnership with the firm back in February; before that, Game Point laid off this kind of risk through specialist reinsurance at places like Lloyd's of London. Now the hedge just lives on a public exchange where anyone can see it. Similar third-party trades showed up on South Carolina's season a month earlier.

Do the math on the first rung and the machinery is beautiful: if LSU makes the playoff, the position pays $837,500 — more than covering the $750,000 bonus check the school owes its coach for getting there. Every deeper run pays more, exactly as the bonus obligation grows. If Kiffin celebrates, the tickets cash. Heads, LSU wins; tails, the market pays.

This is the part of the story the pre-bet desk exists for: betting markets aren't just where fans sweat anymore — they're infrastructure. A university's insurance company is functionally long LSU football, in public, at prices you can look up. The same markets you can trade are now settling coach bonuses.

So when you watch LSU this season, know that you're not the only one with a position. The school's own hedge is riding every snap — and on Fade, you can see which way the money leans before you make your own call.
Sources: The Athletic (NYT), CBS Sports, InGame — reporting on Game Point Capital's Kalshi block trades tied to Lane Kiffin's LSU bonuses, September 2026.

articles.title: College football's biggest loser: Clay Travis opens the season 2–8
articles.dek: Eleven public picks, two winners — and tonight he's doubling down on Florida State +3. The most fadeable card in sports media is back, and the fade army is already counting its money.
articles.author: Fade Desk
body: Every fall it happens on schedule: Clay Travis posts his college football card for the world to see, and the internet does the profitable thing — the exact opposite.

Week 1 of 2026 was a masterpiece of the genre. Eleven picks went up. Georgia Tech -6.5, missed. Stanford +24.5, missed. Texas State +29.5, missed. Baylor/Auburn over 58.5, missed. Furman +46.5, missed. Northern Illinois +31.5, missed. Clemson +10, missed. Wisconsin +20.5, missed.

The survivors: UCLA -1.5 cashed, and the Louisville/Ole Miss over 55.5 snuck through. And the card isn't done — tonight, Clay is on Florida State +3. Same season, same energy, one more chance to do the profitable thing.

None of this is new. The receipts account @ExposingClay has been documenting the run for years, and by Clay's own admission his 2024 season closed at 74–90. There are bad bettors, and then there are bettors so reliably wrong that betting against them becomes its own strategy.

That strategy has a name. It's the whole reason this app exists. When the next card drops, you'll see it in Fade the moment it's posted — with a Tail button for the brave and a Fade button for the rest of us.
Source: @ExposingClay on X — x.com/ExposingClay/status/2096936385051517169. Records reflect publicly posted picks.

articles.title: Case File No. 001 — The Drake Curse
articles.dek: The biggest artist in the world is also the most public bettor alive — eight-figure stakes, posted slips, and a curse so consistent it has its own website.
articles.author: Fade Cases

picks.t: UFC 229: walks McGregor out. Khabib wins

body: Teams he backs crumble. Fighters he walks out lose. The internet keeps the receipts — and there are a lot of receipts.

It got its name at UFC 229, when Drake walked Conor McGregor to the cage and Khabib mauled him. Since then the pattern has been documented in eight figures: a reported million on Argentina to win the World Cup final in regulation — they won the Cup, on penalties, and the bet lost anyway. Seven figures on Israel Adesanya, stopped in the fifth. $400K on Jake Paul against Tommy Fury, gone. $355K on a 58-year-old Mike Tyson, gone.
The one week the curse took off: roughly $700K on the Chiefs in Super Bowl LVII, which cashed. One reported winner. Six reported losers. A body of work so consistent that thedrakecurse.com exists.

This is what a case file is for. On Fade, records like this aren't vibes — they're graded, timestamped, and attached to alerts. Get notified the next time Drake places a bet, and do the profitable thing.
Sources: publicly reported wagers, thedrakecurse.com, Covers. Amounts as reported.

articles.title: Case File No. 002 — El Presidente
articles.dek: Dave Portnoy bets the way he runs Barstool — loudly, publicly, and in seven figures. A 30% hit rate that's somehow up $2.7 million.
articles.author: Fade Cases

picks.t: $1M — Bills to win Super Bowl LIX
$1,000 side bet with Urban Meyer on Michigan

body: Across 30 publicly reported wagers, Dave Portnoy's record is 9–21. That's a 30% hit rate. He is also up $2.7 million. Both facts are true, and both facts are why America watches every slip he posts.

The losses are operatic — $500K on Virginia Tech as a +220 dog, a million on the Bills' Super Bowl that never came, even a $1,000 side bet with Urban Meyer that found a way to lose. But the wins are all-timers: $600K on UConn at +360 to run back the national title, $300K on Scottie Scheffler at +450 the week he put on the green jacket, a Caitlin Clark triple-double at 13-to-1.
That's the Portnoy paradox: fade the volume, respect the futures. A record this loud deserves to be graded live, not argued about on Twitter.
Get notified when El Presidente fires next — tail the future, fade the dog, your call.
Sources: publicly reported and DraftKings-confirmed wagers, 2021–2025. The full 30-bet ledger is graded in Fade.

articles.title: Case File No. 003 — The Houston Hedge
articles.dek: Jim 'Mattress Mack' McIngvale is 3–17 across $86 million in reported stakes — and up $23.5 million anyway, including the largest payout in U.S. betting history.
articles.author: Fade Cases
body: Jim McIngvale bets like nobody else on earth: nine-figure furniture promotions hedged with the biggest sportsbook wagers ever written. When Mack bets, the whole city of Houston sweats with him.

The tracked record reads 3–17 across roughly $86 million in reported stakes — and he's up $23.5 million. That's not a typo; it's a hedge. Every giant ticket backs a 'win your mattress free' promotion, so the sportsbook money and the store money are two sides of one trade.

The crown jewel: $10 million across five books on the 2022 Astros at long prices. Houston won the World Series and the tickets paid $72.6 million — the largest payout in U.S. legal betting history. The scar tissue: $13M gone on the 2019 Astros, $9.5M on the Bengals, $8M on the 2023 runback, $3.3M on the Patriots in Super Bowl LX.
He's the rare case file stamped TAIL: not because the record is pretty, but because the structure wins. Know the difference — that's the whole game.
Sources: publicly reported wagers, 2019–2026. The full 20-bet ledger is graded in Fade.

articles.title: Case File No. 004 — Book It With Trent
articles.dek: Trent Attyah did what no bettor had done before: turned getting faded into a career. The self-made Fade God.
articles.author: Fade Cases

picks.t: The community starts betting the opposite
Surgical streams: the parlay built live on air

body: There are bad bettors, and then there is Trent Attyah — the first man to look at a losing streak and see a business model.

It started in 2021, when a run of losses went so viral that the internet began betting the opposite of every pick he posted. Most people would log off. Trent leaned in: he named it, branded it, and built BookIt Sports around it. The Fade God was born.

The surgical streams are the masterpiece — followers submit picks live on air and Trent assembles the day's parlay from the best of them, 260,000-plus people watching every slip. Every pick is content. Every fade cashes twice: once at the book, once in the culture.
He's the patron saint of this entire app. Get notified when Trent posts, and do what the internet taught us all to do.
Source: the public record, extensively. Founder of BookIt Sports.
